BeliefGraph-JEPA: Structured Latent World Models for Action-Conditioned Time Series

Yue Li Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Kangqi Ni Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill    Zhen Tan Affiliation: Stevens Institute of Technology    Tianlong Chen Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Abstract

Action-conditioned time-series forecasting requires accounting for how future actions and exogenous forcings influence multiple targets through partially observed effects with different delays and persistence. Direct conditioning leaves the evolution and target-specific influence of these effects implicit in the predictor, while static relational graphs specify connections without tracking evolving effects. This motivates representing future-driver influence through structured latent states that evolve over the forecast horizon and route information to individual targets. We introduce BeliefGraph-JEPA, a structured latent world model that factorizes driver influence into typed latent-effect states. These states are rolled forward under future drivers and routed through a graph to target-specific nodes, forming the predictive base of a joint-embedding predictive architecture. A capacity-controlled residual supplements this base with direct driver information. On four multi-target clinical, agricultural, environmental, and industrial systems, the framework outperforms a range of pretrained and supervised known-future-covariate baselines. Matched controls isolate latent dynamics, future rollout, graph routing, and residual capacity; future rollout and graph-first residual routing improve forecasting across all four systems.

   

1 Introduction

Action-conditioned time-series forecasting predicts how future actions and exogenous forcings influence multiple targets. In clinical, agricultural, environmental, and industrial systems, a propofol infusion, a ventilation setpoint, a chemical dose, or a heating-valve command is a driver: an input that acts through delayed, persistent, mechanism-specific hidden effects. Actions are controllable inputs; exogenous forcings are inputs the system cannot set.

Those effects are only partially observed and target-specific: blood pressure and anesthetic depth respond to the same infusion with different lags, while indoor temperature, humidity, CO2, and light evolve together under actuators and outdoor weather.

The question is how to represent known future drivers whose effects are delayed, mechanism-specific, and shared across multiple targets. Covariate-aware and pretrained forecasters [1, 2, 3, 4] and relational variants [5] incorporate available drivers as covariates, tokens, or relational inputs. Other approaches combine action-conditioned prediction with rollout or residual corrections [6, 7]. Across these approaches, typed driver-mediated latent effects remain implicit, as schematized in Figure 1(a). Graph-based forecasters model dependencies among observed series [8, 9], but adjacency alone does not specify how driver-mediated latent effects evolve. Latent world models already roll generic states forward under future actions [10, 11, 12]. Our approach factorizes driver influence into typed latent-effect states, rolls them forward under future drivers, and routes them through a graph to target-specific nodes, using the structured trajectory as the predictive base (Figure 1(b)).

BeliefGraph-JEPA is a structured latent world model organized around a pathway: driver →\rightarrow mechanism-specific latent effect →\rightarrow observed target. A domain-informed typed graph supplies a relational prior. Past drivers initialize mechanism-specific latent-effect states, and a relation-aware GNN reads out their horizon-specific evolution as target-specific graph representations. Actions and exogenous forcings share one driver interface. The graph represents the structured driver-mediated component of the partially observed system, while the neural history representation captures remaining unstructured factors. Graph-first residual routing (GR) uses these graph representations together with observation history to form the predictive base in JEPA space [13, 14]. Direct driver tokens enter only through a gated residual adapter; a residual-magnitude penalty and graph-base supervision constrain the correction.

We evaluate this framework on four multi-target systems with shared driver-mediated mechanisms: intraoperative vital signs (VitalDB) [15], an autonomous greenhouse (Greenhouse) [16], wastewater nutrient control (Wastewater) [17], and a district-heating substation (PreDist) [18] (Table 1).

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Structured latent driver dynamics. We factor future-driver influence into typed latent-effect states and roll those states forward before target-specific graph routing; that structured trajectory is the predictive base. On a matched-dynamics system, this rollout recovers the correct persistence ordering and exhibits pathway-specific impulse responses.

  • •

    Graph-first residual routing. The graph pathway is the predictive base. Direct drivers enter only through a gated residual, whose contribution is constrained by a residual-magnitude penalty and graph-base supervision.

  • •

    Mechanism-oriented evaluation. We use four multi-target systems with shared driver-mediated mechanisms and matched controls that separately test latent dynamics, future rollout, graph structure, and residual capacity.

2 Related Work

Action-conditioned forecasting and known-future covariates. Covariate-aware forecasters send known future actions or exogenous inputs into the predictor. DeepAR, Temporal Fusion Transformer, and TiDE condition on known future covariates [1, 2, 19]; TimeXer attends over historically observed exogenous variables [3]. Foundation models such as Chronos and TimesFM learn strong history extrapolation [20, 21]; Chronos-2, ChronosX, and UniCA extend this line to future-known and heterogeneous covariates [4, 22, 23]. ExoTimer integrates exogenous information with LLM-based text representations [24], and DAG injects discovered endogenous–exogenous correlations into the same forecast [5]. CEDAR augments action-conditioned rollout with event residuals [6]; DRIFT adds recursive action-conditioned corrections to direct forecasts [7]. BeliefGraph-JEPA represents driver influence through typed latent effects, rolled forward and routed to target-specific graph nodes, with the structured trajectory as the predictive base.

Latent world models, state-space models, and JEPA. Model-based control learns action-conditioned latent transitions zt+1=F⁡(zt,at)z_{t+1}=F(z_{t},a_{t}) and rolls them forward under future actions [10, 11, 12, 25]. Structured and selective state-space models provide efficient sequence backbones [26, 27]. Joint-embedding predictive architectures predict in representation space [13, 28, 29], including time series, command-conditioned control, and glucose representation learning [14, 30, 31]. Phys-JEPA decomposes physical versus residual latent content [32]; Delta-JEPA reconstructs actions from latent differences to encourage action-sensitive transitions [33]. Our rollout is factorized by typed driver-mediated effect families and routed to target-specific graph nodes, so future drivers enter as inputs to structured latent mechanisms rather than only as predictor covariates.

Graph-structured and neuro-symbolic world models. Graph neural forecasters learn or assume adjacency among observed variables [8, 9, 34]; GCGNet uses graph consistency over endogenous–exogenous correlations  [35]. LLM-constructed variable-level knowledge graphs add a static semantic prior over the same series [36]. Graph world models use message passing over structured states with action nodes [37]; causal representation models impose directed factor structure on static generative latents [38]. Neuro-symbolic world models learn predicates and abstract dynamics for robot planning [39, 40], and medical trajectory world models simulate clinical courses in language [41]. Our BeliefGraph-JEPA uses a typed graph to organize the driver–effect–target pathway for action-conditioned forecasting.

3 Problem Formulation

At forecast anchor tt, the model is given an observed context Xt−LX+1:t=(xt−LX+1,…,xt)X_{t-L_{X}+1:t}=(x_{t-L_{X}+1},\ldots,x_{t}) of length LXL_{X}, with xτ∈ℝdxx_{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} at each time τ\tau. The task is the continuation Yt+1:t+H=Xt+1:t+HY_{t+1:t+H}=X_{t+1:t+H}. The system is driven by Dτ={Aτ,Eτ}D_{\tau}=\{A_{\tau},\,E_{\tau}\}, where AτA_{\tau} contains controllable actions and EτE_{\tau} contains uncontrollable exogenous forcings. The model is conditioned on future actions over the prediction horizon; in our retrospective experiments, these are the logged actions. Future exogenous inputs, when used, hold the last context value (Table 1). Drivers act through delayed, mechanism-specific hidden effects. Those effects are represented as typed latent states and evolved under future drivers. We treat the setting as a partially observed controlled dynamical system. The model represents the structured driver-mediated component by typed latent-effect states ZtFZ_{t}^{F}, a deterministic summary of past driver effects that is evolved under future drivers and routed to observed targets. Remaining unstructured factors are captured by the neural history representation.

Joint-embedding prediction is performed in representation space [13, 14]. An online context encoder EθE_{\theta} maps the observed history to HtXH_{t}^{X}. An exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder Eθ¯E_{\bar{\theta}} encodes the future sequence, zt+1:t+H∗=sg(Eθ¯(Xt+1:t+H))z_{t+1:t+H}^{*}=\operatorname{sg}\!\bigl(E_{\bar{\theta}}(X_{t+1:t+H})\bigr), with sg\operatorname{sg} the stop-gradient. A predictor produces z^t+1:t+H\hat{z}_{t+1:t+H} from HtXH_{t}^{X}, past drivers, and available future drivers Dt:t+H−1D_{t:t+H-1}. An observation decoder maps z^t+h\hat{z}_{t+h} to y^t+h\hat{y}_{t+h}. The latent and observation objectives are

ℒJEPA=1H​∑h=1H‖z^t+h−zt+h∗‖22,ℒobs=1H​∑h=1H‖y^t+h−yt+h‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\|\hat{z}_{t+h}-z_{t+h}^{*}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\|\hat{y}_{t+h}-y_{t+h}\|_{2}^{2}. (1)

The base objective is ℒ=ℒJEPA+λobs​ℒobs\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obs}}. Section 4 instantiates the predictor by rolling ZtFZ_{t}^{F} under subsequent drivers and using the resulting graph trajectory as the predictive base.

4 Method

BeliefGraph-JEPA has two parts (Figure 2). Section 4.1 turns a typed driver–effect–target prior into typed latent-effect states and rolls them under future drivers. Section 4.2 makes the resulting horizon-specific trajectory the predictive base, with direct driver information entering as a capacity-controlled residual. Implementation details are in Appendix F.

4.1 Typed Latent-Effect Dynamics and Graph Rollout

Typed relational prior. We assume a sparse typed relational prior Gstatic=(VD,VF,VY,ℰ)G_{\mathrm{static}}=(V_{D},V_{F},V_{Y},\mathcal{E}) with VD=VA∪VEV_{D}=V_{A}\cup V_{E}, where VAV_{A}, VEV_{E}, VFV_{F}, and VYV_{Y} are action, exogenous, latent-effect, and target nodes. ℰ\mathcal{E} contains the directed driver→\rightarroweffect and effect→\rightarrowtarget edges, each with a relation label, sign, and confidence. An instantaneous-effect head extends the readout to contemporaneous algebraic targets on PreDist (Appendix E). The prior names which driver families may update which latent effects, and which effects may reach which targets, while sample-specific magnitude and temporal state are learned. VEV_{E} is a domain-selected exogenous subset; exogenous channels not placed in VEV_{E} remain available as direct predictor tokens. Appendix L records the frozen LLM-assisted construction used in experiments.

Unified driver representation. Actions and exogenous forcings share the interface Dτ={Aτ,Eτ}D_{\tau}=\{A_{\tau},E_{\tau}\} and the same output dimension. Encoders keep three attributes separate: numeric type (categorical versus continuous), temporal modality (impulse versus continuous forcing), and role (controllable versus exogenous). Each encoded driver yields a token for the predictor and a latent drive uτu_{\tau} that updates mechanism-specific effect states. Impulse events are one-shot jumps; continuous forcings remain active over physical time. Concurrent drives of the same family and modality are summed. Exogenous graph nodes are refreshed from observed history and, over the horizon, from the last context value; persistence lives in the effect state.

Current graph belief. For latent-effect family ff and a generic time τ\tau, impulse and continuous drives update a recurrent state

zf,τ+1=λf⊙zf,τ+αfimp⊙ϕfimp​(uf,τimp)+(1−λf)⊙αfcont⊙ϕfcont​(uf,τcont),z_{f,\tau+1}=\lambda_{f}\odot z_{f,\tau}+\alpha_{f}^{\mathrm{imp}}\odot\phi_{f}^{\mathrm{imp}}(u_{f,\tau}^{\mathrm{imp}})+(1-\lambda_{f})\odot\alpha_{f}^{\mathrm{cont}}\odot\phi_{f}^{\mathrm{cont}}(u_{f,\tau}^{\mathrm{cont}}), (2)

with σ\sigma the sigmoid and λf=σ⁡(ρf)∈(0,1)\lambda_{f}=\sigma(\rho_{f})\in(0,1) a learned per-family persistence, αfimp\alpha_{f}^{\mathrm{imp}} and αfcont\alpha_{f}^{\mathrm{cont}} learned injection scales in (0,1)(0,1), and ϕfimp\phi_{f}^{\mathrm{imp}}, ϕfcont\phi_{f}^{\mathrm{cont}} pointwise maps of the encoded drives. The impulse term is a state jump followed by decay. The continuous term is stable first-order forcing; (1−λf)(1-\lambda_{f}) keeps a constant input from being amplified as persistence approaches one. Past drivers Dt−LA:t−1D_{t-L_{A}:t-1} are rolled through Eq. (2) from a zero initial state to the forecast anchor tt. The packed family-effect state ZtF=(zf,t)f∈VFZ_{t}^{F}=(z_{f,t})_{f\in V_{F}} factorizes driver influence by mechanism family. The latent-effect window LAL_{A} equals the context length LXL_{X}.

At the forecast anchor, a gate injects each family state into its static node embedding efstatice_{f}^{\mathrm{static}},

hf,τ(0)=efstatic+γf​WfG​zf,τ,γf=σ⁡(δf).h_{f,\tau}^{(0)}=e_{f}^{\mathrm{static}}+\gamma_{f}W_{f}^{G}z_{f,\tau},\qquad\gamma_{f}=\sigma(\delta_{f}). (3)

The injection γf​WfG​zf,τ\gamma_{f}W_{f}^{G}z_{f,\tau} keeps the magnitude of zf,τz_{f,\tau}, which encodes accumulation under the recurrence. History updates zf,τz_{f,\tau} at every step and applies Eq. (3) to the anchor state zf,tz_{f,t}. Ht(0)H_{t}^{(0)} initializes every node: effect nodes carry this injection, and action and exogenous nodes carry their encoded driver features. A two-layer relation-aware GNN [42, 43] then propagates along GstaticG_{\mathrm{static}}, HtG=GNN⁡(Gstatic,Ht(0))H_{t}^{G}=\operatorname{GNN}(G_{\mathrm{static}},H_{t}^{(0)}). Action and exogenous neighbors of an effect node send role-conditioned messages; the two aggregates are concatenated before the effect update. Target nodes receive messages from these effect representations. Thus HtGH_{t}^{G} is the GNN readout of ZtFZ_{t}^{F}, and the current graph belief is the pair (ZtF,HtG)(Z_{t}^{F},H_{t}^{G}).

Future latent-effect rollout. ZtFZ_{t}^{F} summarizes drivers through time t−1t{-}1. The same per-family transition (Eq. 2) is applied causally under subsequent drivers. Writing ℱ\mathcal{F} for that map on the packed family state, Zt+hF=ℱ⁡(Zt+h−1F,Dt+h−1)Z_{t+h}^{F}=\mathcal{F}(Z_{t+h-1}^{F},D_{t+h-1}) for h=1,…,Hh=1,\ldots,H, the horizon-hh state is obtained from ZtFZ_{t}^{F} and Dt:t+h−1D_{t:t+h-1}. Each Zt+hFZ_{t+h}^{F} is injected by Eq. (3), and action and exogenous nodes at that step carry encodings of Dt+h−1D_{t+h-1}. The same GNN returns the horizon-specific readout Ht+hGH_{t+h}^{G}. Latent recurrence is sequential and lightweight. The HH GNN evaluations are independent given {Zt+hF}\{Z_{t+h}^{F}\} and these driver encodings, and are batched over the horizon. Future exogenous inputs hold the last context value (Section 3).

History HtXH_{t}^{X}, the anchor graph HtGH_{t}^{G}, and the horizon readout Ht+hGH_{t+h}^{G} enter a predictor PP with encoded tokens of the future drivers Dt:t+h−1D_{t:t+h-1}, z^t+h=P(HtX,HtG,Ht+hG,Dt:t+h−1,Qh)\hat{z}_{t+h}=P(H_{t}^{X},\,H_{t}^{G},\,H_{t+h}^{G},\,D_{t:t+h-1},\,Q_{h}), where QhQ_{h} is a learned query embedding for horizon hh. The horizon queries are decoded jointly, with query hh using Ht+hGH_{t+h}^{G} and the driver prefix Dt:t+h−1D_{t:t+h-1}. We call this architecture future rollout (FR).

4.2 Structured Rollout as the Predictive Base

FR lets the horizon graph readout and encoded future driver tokens enter one predictor. GR designates the graph-mediated trajectory as the predictive base zt+hG=PG​(HtX,HtG,Ht+hG,Qh)z_{t+h}^{G}=P_{G}(H_{t}^{X},\,H_{t}^{G},\,H_{t+h}^{G},\,Q_{h}). The base zt+hGz_{t+h}^{G} is a JEPA-space prediction. History HtXH_{t}^{X} and the anchor graph HtGH_{t}^{G} enter PGP_{G} with the horizon readout Ht+hGH_{t+h}^{G}. Future drivers reach this base through the rollout Zt+hF=ℱ⁡(Zt+h−1F,Dt+h−1)Z_{t+h}^{F}=\mathcal{F}(Z_{t+h-1}^{F},D_{t+h-1}) and the subsequent GNN, so PGP_{G} conditions on them through Ht+hGH_{t+h}^{G}. Encoded tokens of Dt:t+h−1D_{t:t+h-1} enter a residual adapter ARA_{R} with a stop-gradient copy of this base, Δzt+hR=AR(HtX,Dt:t+h−1,sg(zt+hG),Qh)\Delta z_{t+h}^{R}=A_{R}(H_{t}^{X},\,D_{t:t+h-1},\,\operatorname{sg}(z_{t+h}^{G}),\,Q_{h}). The prediction is then

z^t+h=zt+hG+αR​Δ​zt+hR,αR=αmaxR​σ​(a),\hat{z}_{t+h}=z_{t+h}^{G}+\alpha^{R}\Delta z_{t+h}^{R},\qquad\alpha^{R}=\alpha^{R}_{\max}\,\sigma(a), (4)

where αmaxR<1\alpha^{R}_{\max}<1 is a fixed cap and aa is a learned scalar. The residual adapter is zero-initialized, so training begins from z^t+h≈zt+hG\hat{z}_{t+h}\approx z_{t+h}^{G}.

Graph-base supervision trains the base to match the JEPA target on its own, and a residual-magnitude penalty keeps the residual a correction,

ℒG=1H​∑h=1H‖zt+hG−zt+h∗‖22,ℒcap=1H​∑h=1H‖αR​Δ​zt+hR‖22.\mathcal{L}_{G}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\|z_{t+h}^{G}-z_{t+h}^{*}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\|\alpha^{R}\Delta z_{t+h}^{R}\|_{2}^{2}. (5)

The training objective extends the base objective to ℒ=ℒJEPA+λG​ℒG+λcap​ℒcap+λobs​ℒobs\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}}+\lambda_{G}\,\mathcal{L}_{G}+\lambda_{\mathrm{cap}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{obs}}. Residual reliance is the magnitude of the gated correction relative to the combined magnitude of the base and correction,

ρR=1H​∑h=1H‖αR​Δ​zt+hR‖2‖zt+hG‖2+‖αR​Δ​zt+hR‖2+ε.\rho_{R}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{\|\alpha^{R}\Delta z_{t+h}^{R}\|_{2}}{\|z_{t+h}^{G}\|_{2}+\|\alpha^{R}\Delta z_{t+h}^{R}\|_{2}+\varepsilon}. (6)

where ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a small constant. Because ARA_{R} learns the scale of Δ​zt+hR\Delta z_{t+h}^{R}, reliance is read from ρR\rho_{R} rather than from the gate αR\alpha^{R}. The main method is FR-GR, which uses future rollout as the graph base and a capacity-controlled residual on that base.

5 Experiments

Table 1 lists the four multi-target protocols, in each of which several targets share typed driver-mediated mechanisms. For retrospective evaluation, all action-conditioned methods receive the same logged future actions. Future exogenous inputs, when present, hold the last context value over the horizon. Sampling grids and forecast windows are in Table 6; preprocessing and training settings are in Appendix B and Appendix G.

Metrics and controls. Primary metrics are pooled normalized MAE and RMSE on the [−1,1][-1,1] target scale, reported as mean ±\pm sample standard deviation over three seeds {42,43,44}\{42,43,44\}. Baselines are last-value persistence, history-only Chronos-2 and TimesFM 2.5, and covariate-aware Chronos-2-Cov, DAG, and TFT, the last three with oracle future actions and future exogenous inputs held at the last context value [4, 21, 5, 2]. The sections below isolate latent dynamics, future rollout, graph structure, and residual capacity in turn.

5.1 Overall forecasting performance

Table 2 reports the four-system comparison; per-target physical-unit errors are in Appendix D. TFT is one of the most competitive external baselines in our experiments and uses the same constructed-exogenous and oracle-action future protocol as DAG and BeliefGraph-JEPA. FR-GR attains lower nMAE and nRMSE on Greenhouse, VitalDB, and PreDist; TFT attains slightly lower nMAE on Wastewater, with nRMSE essentially tied. Per-target gains vary across variables (Appendix D): FR-GR attains the lowest mean MAE and RMSE on Greenhouse indoor temperature, humidity, and CO2, and on VitalDB BIS; on PreDist, it also improves over TFT on heat power and flow.

To isolate where those gains arise, a cumulative ladder adds one module at a time up to FR: history only (HO), future-driver tokens (DC), a static typed GNN (SG), instant effect nodes without temporal persistence (IE), and a current recurrent belief without future rollout (RB). Direct future-driver conditioning already provides a gain over history-only prediction: DC improves over HO on all four systems, most clearly on Greenhouse and Wastewater. A static typed GNN adds little beyond those tokens. Persistent latent-effect dynamics then improve consistently: RB improves over IE on every dataset, and rolling those states forward under future drivers improves again: FR improves over RB.

flat keeps the FR predictor but replaces GNN message passing with an unstructured aggregation of effect states. flat-GR applies the same base–residual decomposition, auxiliary base supervision, and residual-capacity penalty to that unstructured readout. UR-GR keeps the flat-GR readout and residual routing, and replaces the family-specific latent states with one shared state. RB-GR applies the same design to the current-belief model. flat stays close to FR, indicating that much of the forecasting benefit is retained without GNN message passing. This design improves both readouts: flat-GR over flat, and FR-GR over FR. FR-GR also improves over RB-GR, supporting future rollout under matched residual routing. UR-GR performs similarly to flat-GR overall. FR-GR achieves lower mean errors than UR-GR on all four datasets; its gains over flat-GR are clearest on Greenhouse, smaller on PreDist, and limited on Wastewater and VitalDB. These results indicate dataset-dependent gains from explicit graph routing. The remaining diagnostics use FR-GR as the main method.

5.2 Making structured rollout the predictive base

Table 3 compares fusion controls. FR fuses the graph trajectory and direct future drivers in one predictor. A hard graph bottleneck (HB) uses the same predictor but withholds graph-covered future-driver tokens from the direct path. FR-GR-GO evaluates the FR-GR graph base at αR=0\alpha^{R}=0; FR-GR-U uses αR=1\alpha^{R}=1 and no residual-capacity penalty.

On all four datasets, HB matches or slightly improves upon FR: graph-covered future driver information can be carried through the rolled graph pathway without those tokens on the direct path. The graph-only readout FR-GR-GO stays close to FR on Greenhouse and PreDist, so the rolled graph trajectory is already a structured predictive base. Removing the residual from FR-GR raises error on every dataset, so the direct correction still captures information beyond that base. An unrestricted residual (FR-GR-U) improves over FR on every dataset: graph-first prediction helps even without a residual-capacity penalty. Capacity control further improves Greenhouse, Wastewater, and PreDist, while FR-GR and FR-GR-U remain comparable on VitalDB. For FR-GR, the relative residual magnitude ρR\rho_{R} is 1.41.4–3.9%3.9\% (Appendix I). FR-GR also outperforms HB on all four datasets: a capacity-controlled residual complements the graph base better than a hard bottleneck.

5.3 What does graph structure contribute?

Where Table 2 varies whether readout is a typed GNN, Table 4 holds the FR-GR backbone fixed and varies which typed graph is used, by changing it during retraining or only at inference. These controls use Greenhouse and Wastewater, where the domain prior is sparse and a typed fully-connected alternative is well-defined. Panel A retrains FR-GR with a learned fully-connected graph (LFC) and a pre-specified slot-shuffled prior that remaps driver→\rightarroweffect slot inputs while keeping effect→\rightarrowtarget edges fixed. Panel B swaps the prior only at evaluation, testing the domain-graph checkpoint under the slot shuffle and the slot-shuffled checkpoint under the domain graph.

The domain graph attains the lowest error on both datasets. A learned fully-connected graph is worse, especially on Greenhouse, supporting the sparse typed prior over learning connectivity from a complete graph. Slot-shuffled retraining stays close, indicating that an alternative typed routing remains competitive after retraining. In contrast, swapping the same assignment only at inference raises error sharply, especially on Wastewater (nMAE 0.12450.1245 to 0.16100.1610); the reverse swap also increases error. The typed graph is therefore a relational inductive bias: predictions use the routing learned during training, while an alternative typed assignment remains competitive once retrained. The remaining experiments examine how the routed belief evolves under future drivers.

5.4 Can future rollout recover matched latent-effect dynamics?

Real forecasting data do not reveal ground-truth latent-effect states or persistences, and Appendix J shows that multiple persistence configurations can achieve nearly identical forecast error. We therefore probe capacity on a matched leaky-integrator with known fast and slow latent mechanisms: a class-matched check of whether future rollout recovers distinct persistences and pathway-specific driver-to-target responses (Figure 3, Table 3; Appendix K).

The two wired effect families have λfast=0.40\lambda_{\mathrm{fast}}=0.40 and λslow=0.75\lambda_{\mathrm{slow}}=0.75, both initialized at 0.5750.575. Correct recovery therefore requires the learned persistences to move in opposite directions. A third driver has no target path and serves as a null control. Superscript id\mathrm{id} denotes the matched protocol of Appendix K, which isolates future driver-to-latent dynamics by restricting direct prediction shortcuts.

Figure 3 reports learned persistences against the shared initialization and the two ground-truth scales. Table 3 reports the corresponding peak driver-to-target pulse responses. Without future rollout, RBid leaves the two persistences nearly equal and produces no pulse response. FRid (HB) recovers the correct ordering (0.449<0.6410.449<0.641) and halves MAE from 0.0630.063 to 0.0310.031, but only the fast pathway responds (0.3710.371); the slow pathway stays near zero. FR-GRid moves the estimates further toward the ground truth (0.429<0.6790.429<0.679), reduces MAE to 0.0130.013, and recovers both wired responses (0.4300.430 and 0.1410.141), with off-path and null channels near zero. Among the compared variants, future rollout recovers the correct persistence ordering, while the full FR-GRid model exhibits responses on both wired pathways, including the slow pathway. Appendix K.4 examines a saturating tanh\tanh mismatch: the slow-path response remains near zero at 4040 epochs but increases at 8080 epochs, while both response magnitudes remain underestimated.

5.5 Do forecasts use future actions?

Figure 5 reports an input-dependence diagnostic: error sensitivity to later actions (Appendix H). At evaluation we add a fixed signed offset to every continuous future-action channel on the second half of the horizon, hold exogenous inputs and categorical actions fixed, and report the percent nMAE increase Δperturb=(nMAEperturb−nMAEclean)/nMAEclean\Delta_{\mathrm{perturb}}=(\mathrm{nMAE}_{\mathrm{perturb}}-\mathrm{nMAE}_{\mathrm{clean}})/\mathrm{nMAE}_{\mathrm{clean}} on the full window.

On Greenhouse, Wastewater, and VitalDB, DC and RB show only weak sensitivity to the second-half offset: Δperturb\Delta_{\mathrm{perturb}} is 0.70.7–4.6%4.6\%, despite DC receiving future-driver tokens directly. Explicitly rolling the latent-effect belief under those later drivers produces a much larger forecast-error increase: 7.2%7.2\%, 18.1%18.1\%, and 12.1%12.1\%. RB-GR is intermediate (3.5%3.5\%, 7.1%7.1\%, 4.1%4.1\%): the residual adapter sees the perturbed tokens, while the graph base remains the current belief. FR-GR matches or exceeds FR on Greenhouse (7.7%7.7\% versus 7.2%7.2\%) and remains comparable on Wastewater (17.2%17.2\% versus 18.1%18.1\%), and remains an order of magnitude above RB on VitalDB (9.8%9.8\% versus 1.0%1.0\%). On PreDist, Δperturb\Delta_{\mathrm{perturb}} is already 28.8%28.8\% for DC. Future rollout still produces the largest error increase (65.4%65.4\% for FR, 72.9%72.9\% for FR-GR). Future rollout therefore makes predictions depend on later actions, including offsets that token-only conditioning largely ignores.

5.6 Horizon-wise benefit of future rollout

Figure 5 reports per-horizon nMAE relative to DC. Negative values are lower error. FR-GR is lowest at every lead time. Across all four datasets, FR and FR-GR generally outperform their current-belief counterparts, RB and RB-GR, across lead times. The gap widens with lead time on Greenhouse and Wastewater, most steadily on Greenhouse. On PreDist, FR-GR remains lowest throughout. On VitalDB’s six-minute horizon, FR-GR slightly improves over RB-GR. Together, these comparisons support evolving latent effects under future drivers, with the magnitude of the benefit varying across datasets and lead times.

6 Conclusion

We presented BeliefGraph-JEPA, a structured latent world model for action-conditioned forecasting. Future drivers enter latent dynamics through typed latent-effect states and graph-mediated rollout, with a capacity-controlled residual. On four multi-target systems across distinct domains, the framework outperforms a range of pretrained and supervised known-future-covariate baselines. Explicit graph routing provides additional, dataset-dependent gains. Matched ablations isolate latent dynamics, future rollout, graph routing, and residual capacity. On a matched-dynamics system, the model recovers the correct persistence ordering and exhibits pathway-specific impulse responses. On the real systems, later-action offsets change the forecast once the latent-effect states are rolled forward. Identifying latent mechanisms and extending the framework to action planning remain directions for future work.

Appendix A Datasets

The main evaluation uses four multi-target controlled systems (Table 1, Appendix A.1), in which several targets share typed driver-mediated mechanisms. We apply BeliefGraph-JEPA to two single-target glucose protocols (Table 7, Appendix A.2), where the typed graph has one observed sink and fewer effect-to-target routes. Forecasting results for those protocols are in Appendix C. Per-target breakdowns of the four multi-target systems are in Appendix D. Train/val/test splits and remaining preprocessing are in Appendix B.

A.1 Multi-target datasets

VitalDB. Intraoperative vital signs from surgical cases [15]. Targets are mean arterial pressure, heart rate, pulse oxygen saturation, and bispectral index. Continuous actions are propofol and remifentanil infusion rates. There is no exogenous channel. The same infusion can affect pressure and anesthetic depth with different lags, so the typed graph routes one driver family to several targets.

Greenhouse. The 3rd Autonomous Greenhouse Challenge [16]: lettuce compartments under closed-loop climate control. Targets are indoor air temperature, relative humidity, CO2 concentration, and incoming PAR. Continuous actions are heating-pipe temperature, leeward and windward vents, thermal and shade screens, grow lights, and CO2 dosing. Exogenous inputs are outdoor weather. Future outdoor weather holds the last context value over the horizon.

Wastewater nutrient control. A biological nutrient-removal tank with online sensors and dosing [17]. Targets are dissolved oxygen, ammonium, and phosphate. Continuous actions are metal-salt dosing channels; categorical actions are inlet and outlet process phases. Exogenous inputs are inflow rate and water temperature. Dosing and phase changes persist beyond a single step and affect the three nutrient targets through shared process mechanisms.

PreDist. District-heating substations [18]. Targets include secondary supply temperature, return temperatures, heat power, and flow. Continuous actions are valve position and supply-temperature setpoint; categorical actions include pump status, control mode, and a three-way valve. Exogenous inputs are outdoor temperature and primary-grid supply temperature. Heat power and flow are algebraic: their instantaneous values are determined by contemporaneous temperatures and hydraulic drivers. This protocol mixes delayed inertial targets with same-horizon algebraic targets and uses an instantaneous-effect head (Appendix E).

Table 6 lists the sampling grid and forecast windows.

A.2 Single-target datasets

Table 7 summarizes the two single-target glucose protocols. Both use the same driver–graph–rollout–residual framework as the multi-target systems; there is no exogenous channel.

CGMacros. Continuous glucose monitoring with meal logs [44]. The sole target is interstitial glucose. Actions are sparse meal events with macronutrient annotations; there is no exogenous channel and no dense control input. The typed graph therefore has a single observed target and fewer effect-to-target routes than the multi-target systems above.

Shanghai Diabetes. Shanghai T1DM/T2DM CGM with meal, injection, and oral-drug logs [45]. The sole target is glucose. Actions are sparse clinical events; there is no exogenous channel. As in CGMacros, the graph topology is a single-target driver–effect–glucose routing structure.

Appendix B Dataset preprocessing

Windows never cross session boundaries. A session break is a contiguous invalid-target gap (VitalDB, Greenhouse, Wastewater, PreDist) or a timestamp gap of more than 30 minutes (CGMacros, Shanghai Diabetes). Short sessions and windows whose target NaN ratio exceeds a dataset-specific threshold are dropped. Target and exogenous channels are min-max normalized to [−1,1][-1,1] with fixed physical ranges. Continuous actions use channel-wise min-max. Categorical actions remain integer indices. Nutrition and dose features on the glucose datasets are z-scored from the training split only.

VitalDB. Native recordings are on a 2 s grid and are resampled to 10 s for training. Splits are by surgical case at 70/15/15 with seed 42: the same case never appears in more than one split.

Greenhouse. Splits are by team/compartment with seed 42: two teams are held out for test, one for validation, and the remainder for training. Compartments from the same team stay in the same split.

Wastewater nutrient control. The source is a single plant, so splits are chronological by calendar month at 70/15/15. Earlier months train, later months validate and test; there is no random subject shuffle.

PreDist. Splits are by substation at 70/15/15 with seed 42. Maintenance events are not treated as actions.

CGMacros. Native CGM is 1 min and is resampled to 5 min for training. Splits are by subject at 70/15/15 with seed 42, stratified by A1c phenotype (healthy, prediabetes, type 2 diabetes) so that each phenotype appears in every split when the cohort is large enough.

Shanghai Diabetes. Splits are by subject at 70/10/20 with seed 42, stratified by phenotype (T1DM, T2DM) and then merged. Adjacent records more than 30 minutes apart form distinct sessions.

Appendix C Single-target evaluation

Table 8 applies the HO–FR ladder and its GR variants from Table 2 to the two glucose protocols of Table 7. The typed graph has one observed target, so there are fewer effect-to-target routes than on the four multi-target systems. Metrics are physical-unit MAE and RMSE in mg/dL. Foundation-model rows are single-run; remaining rows are mean ±\pm sample std over three seeds.

On CGMacros, future meal tokens produce the large step: DC lowers MAE from 14.7214.72 (HO) to 13.2413.24. Persistent effects and future rollout add smaller increments. FR-GR attains the lowest MAE and RMSE (12.7612.76 and 19.9519.95), essentially tied with TFT (12.7912.79 and 20.8120.81) and ahead of DAG (13.3713.37) and TimesFM 2.5 (14.8914.89). Relative to HO, that is a 13%13\% MAE reduction.

On Shanghai Diabetes, actions are sparse typed clinical events (meal, injection, oral drug) and the graph has a single glucose sink. TFT attains the lowest MAE and RMSE (15.3015.30 and 23.8823.88), ahead of DAG (15.8815.88). Within the shared ladder, RB-GR is lowest (16.2416.24 MAE, 25.0125.01 RMSE) and FR-GR is 16.5216.52.

Table 9 evaluates the graph base zGz^{G} (αR=0\alpha^{R}{=}0) and the full prediction z^=zG+αR​Δ​zR\hat{z}=z^{G}+\alpha^{R}\Delta z^{R} on the same checkpoints. Residual gain is err⁡(zG)−err⁡(z^)\mathrm{err}(z^{G})-\mathrm{err}(\hat{z}). The residual of RB-GR lowers MAE by 0.860.86. Future rollout improves the graph base by 0.320.32 (zGz^{G} MAE 17.1017.10 to 16.7816.78); the residual of FR-GR then lowers MAE by only 0.250.25. The two mechanisms are substitutes for future-driver information, and the current-belief residual is the stronger route. Future events occupy 40%40\% of Shanghai test windows, so RB-GR already reads those tokens, while rolled ZFZ^{F} is empty on the complementary windows.

The same framework also applies to single-target action-conditioned forecasting. With one observed sink the gain over HO is smaller than in Table 2, and the best GR variant is not the same on both protocols: FR-GR on CGMacros, RB-GR on Shanghai. TFT is essentially tied with FR-GR on CGMacros and is strongest on Shanghai. The strongest benefits of the full framework are observed in the multi-target setting, where several targets share typed driver-mediated mechanisms. A plausible explanation is that multiple effect-to-target routes provide the graph pathway with target-specific routing structure that a single-sink graph does not provide.

Appendix D Per-target evaluation

Table 2 pools every target on the [−1,1][-1,1] scale. Tables 10–13 report physical-unit MAE and RMSE for each target, with the same methods and seeds. Foundation-model rows are single-run; remaining rows are mean ±\pm sample std over seeds {42,43,44}\{42,43,44\}.

Per-target errors reveal where the aggregate gains arise. On Greenhouse, FR-GR is lowest on indoor temperature, humidity, and CO2. TFT is lowest on PAR MAE; UR-GR is lowest on PAR RMSE. On Wastewater, TFT is lowest on DO and PO4 and on NH4 MAE; flat-GR is lowest on NH4 RMSE. On VitalDB, FR-GR is lowest on BIS, a graph-covered drug-sensitive target, and is comparable to flat-GR on MBP. TFT is lowest on HR MAE, while FR-GR is lowest on HR RMSE. SpO2 has no drug-effect edge in the prior (Appendix L), and TimesFM 2.5 attains the lowest MAE. On PreDist, FR-GR is lower than FR, flat-GR, and UR-GR on net-return temperature and heat power, and lower than FR and flat-GR on flow. UR-GR is lowest on supply temperature. TFT is lowest on net-return temperature, and DAG is lower on the algebraic heat-power and flow channels. This distinction is reflected in the role-specific construction of Appendix E: temperatures evolve as inertial states, while heat power and flow are contemporaneous algebraic readouts (Table 14).

Appendix E Instantaneous-effect head

The instantaneous-effect head is an extension for contemporaneous algebraic targets, used on PreDist.

An observation vector can mix two constitutive roles. Delayed inertial targets evolve as states with memory. Instantaneous algebraic targets are contemporaneous functions of those states and of the current drivers. A single JEPA latent zt+hz_{t+h} then packs both roles into one vector. The teacher, the predictor, and the decoder share one interface for a slow state and a same-horizon readout.

The instantaneous-effect head splits that interface by role c∈{dyn,alg}c\in\{\mathrm{dyn},\mathrm{alg}\}. Inertial channels keep family-effect memory through Eq. (2). Algebraic channels are evaluated on the same horizon and never enter ℱ\mathcal{F}. The construction follows the target property: delayed inertial channels together with instantaneous algebraic channels.

PreDist is the evaluation system with this mix. Supply and return temperatures store heat and lag valve, setpoint, and pump changes. Heat power and volume flow are algebraic functions of those temperatures and of the hydraulic drivers at the same 1010 min step. The typed prior follows the same split (Appendix L): GdynG_{\mathrm{dyn}} routes driver→\rightarroweffect→\rightarrowtemperature; GalgG_{\mathrm{alg}} routes valve/pump/three-way→\rightarrowflow and flow+Δ​T→+\Delta T\rightarrowheat power on the same horizon.

Independent observation head. The context encoder remains joint over the history window. The head indexes the EMA teacher, the predictor queries, and the decoder by role. Each role keeps its own JEPA latent, and each decoder head reconstructs only that role’s channels. A shared-latent baseline that packs both roles into one zt+hz_{t+h}, treats algebraic channels as additional inertial states, and decodes every channel from that vector is the comparison in Table 14.

Family persistence λf\lambda_{f}. In Eq. (2), λf=σ⁡(ρf)\lambda_{f}=\sigma(\rho_{f}) is the learned retention of a latent-effect family. It says how long a driver injection remains in zf,τz_{f,\tau}. That persistence is the right object for delayed influence: a valve or setpoint command continues to move inertial temperatures after it is issued. Instantaneous algebraic targets have no such reservoir. Their value at t+ht+h is fixed once contemporaneous inertial states and drivers are known.

The IE ablation removes the λf​zf,τ\lambda_{f}z_{f,\tau} term, so an effect node does not carry driver history. An algebraic observation is not an effect node with λf=0\lambda_{f}=0. It is a constraint on the current inertial state and drivers, and it never enters ZFZ^{F}. Family persistence governs how long those drivers remain available to the inertial targets. The instantaneous-effect head governs how the two kinds of observation are represented in JEPA space.

Construction. Let IdynI_{\mathrm{dyn}} index the inertial channels and IalgI_{\mathrm{alg}} the algebraic channels. On PreDist these are the three temperatures and the pair (heat power, flow). The context encoder EθE_{\theta} remains joint over the full history. The EMA teacher is applied once per role to the same future sequence with a causal mask and complementary channels zeroed:

zt+1:t+H∗,c=sg(Eθ¯(Xt+1:t+Hc)),c∈{dyn,alg},z_{t+1:t+H}^{*,c}=\operatorname{sg}\!\bigl(E_{\bar{\theta}}(X_{t+1:t+H}^{c})\bigr),\qquad c\in\{\mathrm{dyn},\mathrm{alg}\}, (7)

where Xt+1:t+HcX_{t+1:t+H}^{c} equals Xt+1:t+HX_{t+1:t+H} on IcI_{c} and is zero elsewhere, and zt+h∗,cz_{t+h}^{*,c} depends only on Xt+1:t+hcX_{t+1:t+h}^{c}. A shared predictor, and under GR a shared residual adapter, emit z^t+hc\hat{z}_{t+h}^{c} from a role query rcr_{c}. Role identity is that query embedding; driver tokens are shared across roles. When a dual-timescale prior is present, dyn queries attend the GdynG_{\mathrm{dyn}} readout with algebraic nodes zeroed, and alg queries attend the merged GalgG_{\mathrm{alg}} readout. At horizon hh, GdynG_{\mathrm{dyn}} is evaluated from the rolled family states Zt+hFZ_{t+h}^{F}. GalgG_{\mathrm{alg}} then overwrites the action and exogenous nodes with the encodings of Dt+h−1D_{t+h-1} and message-passes on algebraic edges. The heating-circuit return parent of heat power uses that GdynG_{\mathrm{dyn}} embedding as its source: static identity and type, updated by effect-to-temperature messages from those rolled states (Appendix F). Decoder heads map z^t+hdyn\hat{z}_{t+h}^{\mathrm{dyn}} onto IdynI_{\mathrm{dyn}} and z^t+halg\hat{z}_{t+h}^{\mathrm{alg}} onto IalgI_{\mathrm{alg}}. The JEPA term averages the two role residuals. The same driver–graph–rollout–residual stack of Section 4 is used throughout. HO and DC keep the role split without a GNN, reading roles from the channel inventory.

Table 14 compares that head to a shared-latent FR-GR that packs all five PreDist targets into one zt+hz_{t+h}. Removing the head raises pooled nMAE from 0.04950.0495 to 0.05820.0582, above DAG (0.05120.0512) and TimesFM 2.5 (0.05630.0563) in Table 2. The increase is concentrated on the algebraic channels: heat-power MAE rises from 18.8518.85 to 28.5228.52 and flow from 0.5620.562 to 0.7300.730. The three inertial temperatures remain close; heating-circuit return is unchanged. The current shared-latent packing is therefore a worse interface for this mix. The head keeps delayed temperatures and contemporaneous readouts in separate JEPA spaces, and that split recovers the algebraic maps.

Appendix F Architecture details

This appendix records the computational interfaces of Sections 3–4.

EMA teacher. Eθ¯E_{\bar{\theta}} is a momentum-updated copy of EθE_{\theta} with the same architecture. After each optimizer step, every parameter is updated by EMA with decay 0.9960.996. EθE_{\theta} and Eθ¯E_{\bar{\theta}} use the same learned positional embeddings, evaluated at indices 0,…,L−10,\ldots,L{-}1 of their respective input sequences. During training, Eθ¯E_{\bar{\theta}} encodes the ground-truth future sequence Xt+1:t+HX_{t+1:t+H} with a causal mask. Its hh-th output token defines the stop-gradient target zt+h∗z_{t+h}^{*} and depends only on Xt+1:t+hX_{t+1:t+h}. On PreDist, the teacher is applied once per role to the same future sequence with complementary channels zeroed (Appendix E).

Non-effect node features. Every node is initialized as eistatic=eiid+eitypee_{i}^{\mathrm{static}}=e_{i}^{\mathrm{id}}+e_{i}^{\mathrm{type}}. Effect nodes then receive the gated injection of zf,τz_{f,\tau} (Eq. 3). Exogenous nodes are source-only in the prior, so reverse edges into them are omitted; once written, their input encodings are restored after each GNN layer. Target nodes remain at their static embeddings until message passing. The GNN is re-evaluated separately at each horizon using {Zt+hF}h=1H\{Z_{t+h}^{F}\}_{h=1}^{H} and {Dt+h−1}h=1H\{D_{t+h-1}\}_{h=1}^{H}.

On a single-timescale prior, action and exogenous nodes are overwritten with their corresponding encodings from Dt+h−1D_{t+h-1}, the last driver of the rollout prefix, before message passing. Horizon-hh node features therefore comprise static identity and type, rolled family states Zt+hFZ_{t+h}^{F}, and those driver encodings. On a dual-timescale prior, GdynG_{\mathrm{dyn}} is first evaluated from Zt+hFZ_{t+h}^{F} without this horizon-driver overwrite. GalgG_{\mathrm{alg}} then overwrites only action and exogenous nodes with their corresponding encodings from Dt+h−1D_{t+h-1} and message-passes on algebraic edges. On PreDist, the heating-circuit return parent of heat power is read from this GdynG_{\mathrm{dyn}} embedding.

GNN edge attributes. Relation labels become discrete edge types with a learned matrix WrW_{r}. Confidence initializes a learnable scalar gate g=σ⁡(ℓ)g=\sigma(\ell), with ℓ=logit⁡(clip⁡(c,ε,1−ε))\ell=\operatorname{logit}(\operatorname{clip}(c,\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon)). Messages are g​Wr​hsrcg\,W_{r}h_{\mathrm{src}}. Sign is stored as metadata in the prior.

Predictor attention. Query hh conditions on Ht+hGH_{t+h}^{G} by cross-attention to that horizon’s graph nodes. Cross-attention to encoded driver tokens is prefix-masked: query hh attends Dt:t+h−1D_{t:t+h-1}. Under GR, those tokens enter only through ARA_{R}, with the same prefix mask. Horizon queries then share decoder self-attention, with no causal mask among queries. The recurrence is sequential; the decoder is joint over the known-action horizon.

Residual adapter. ARA_{R} is a Transformer decoder over encoded tokens of Dt:t+H−1D_{t:t+H-1} and history HtXH_{t}^{X}. Cross-attention uses the same prefix mask; query self-attention is unmasked. Its last linear layer is zero-initialized.

Appendix G Training configuration

Tables 15–16 record the FR-GR recipe used in Table 2. Wastewater uses 5050 epochs rather than 3030 because validation nMAE continues to decrease through the longer schedule; the remaining datasets use 3030 epochs. The latent-effect window equals the context length LXL_{X} (Table 6). VitalDB uses a matched-window control: windows are indexed as if LA=180L_{A}=180, then past drivers are truncated to LX=90L_{X}=90. Per-family timescales τf\tau_{f} initialize λf\lambda_{f} in steps: VitalDB propofol 24, remifentanil 12; Greenhouse thermal 24, ventilation 6, light 2, screen 4, CO2 6; Wastewater dosing 8, aeration 6, phase 15; PreDist valve 6, setpoint 18, pump 1. A shared τ=8\tau=8 is compared in Appendix J. The glucose protocols in Appendix C use the same FR-GR backbone with batch size 16 and learning rate 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4}; Shanghai uses a typed event encoder and CGMacros a meal encoder.

Parameter counts stay near 22–33M. One run finishes in 0.40.4–44 hours on a single A100, with VitalDB taking the longest. Latent recurrence is sequential in LX+HL_{X}{+}H and linear in |VF||V_{F}|. The HH GNN evaluations are independent given the rolled states and horizon-specific driver encodings, and are batched over the horizon. The history encoder and predictor dominate wall-clock cost.

Appendix H Future-action perturbation protocol

Section 5.5 offsets continuous future-action channels on the second half of the horizon, I=[H/2,H)I=[H/2,H), and reports the relative nMAE increase Δperturb\Delta_{\mathrm{perturb}} on the full window. The offset is applied in the normalized action space used at training. Categorical actions and exogenous inputs are held fixed. Continuous channels admit a shared additive offset of controlled magnitude. Categorical substitutions have no common scale: a label change can be nearly inert or can switch the operating mode. The diagnostic therefore tests whether forecasts use later continuous-action inputs.

Per-channel signs sj∈{+1,−1}s_{j}\in\{+1,-1\} are drawn once and shared across methods. If more than 10%10\% of steps in II clip for a sample-channel, that sample-channel sign is flipped. Clipped values remain in the training range.

Appendix I Residual scale and reliance

Table 18 reports the converged residual scale αR\alpha^{R} and realized residual reliance ρR\rho_{R} of FR-GR. Across datasets, ρR\rho_{R} is 1.41.4–3.9%3.9\%: the residual has small relative latent magnitude compared with the graph base. Removing it at evaluation (FR-GR-GO in Table 3) nevertheless raises nMAE and nRMSE on every dataset; the larger degradation on Greenhouse and Wastewater coincides with their larger ρR\rho_{R}. A small residual is sufficient to recover information omitted by the graph abstraction. Sensitivity of the same quantities to residual-scale initialization and graph-base supervision is in Appendix J.

Appendix J Hyperparameter sensitivity

We evaluate the sensitivity of FR-GR to four design choices across the four multi-target protocols: residual-scale initialization, graph-base supervision weight, latent-effect history length, and family-timescale initialization. All remaining settings follow Appendix G.

Table 19 tests sensitivity to the residual-scale initialization and graph-base supervision weight. Increasing the initial residual scale from αR=0.1\alpha^{R}=0.1 to 0.30.3, or reducing λG\lambda_{G} tenfold from 0.10.1 to 0.010.01, leaves test nMAE and nRMSE essentially unchanged across all four protocols.

Table 20 reports the same residual-scale and reliance quantities as Table 18 under these perturbations. A larger initialization produces a substantially larger converged αR\alpha^{R}, but the realized reliance ρR\rho_{R} remains nearly unchanged. Reducing λG\lambda_{G} likewise has little effect on either forecasting error or residual reliance. Across all settings, ρR\rho_{R} remains in the narrow range 0.0140.014–0.0400.040.

These results distinguish the learned scale parameter from realized residual magnitude: different values of αR\alpha^{R} can produce similar ρR\rho_{R}. The small and stable ρR\rho_{R} shows that the residual remains small in latent magnitude relative to the graph predictive base.

Table 21 tests whether initializing the current latent-effect belief requires driver history preceding the observation context. We set LA=2​LXL_{A}=2L_{X}, adding one full context length of past drivers before the observed history.

Test nMAE and nRMSE remain essentially unchanged on all four protocols. Additional pre-context driver history therefore provides no measurable forecasting benefit. The main model consequently uses context-aligned belief initialization, LA=LXL_{A}=L_{X}, rather than a separate latent-dynamics warm-up window.

Table 22 tests whether the reported forecasting gains depend on the hand-specified family timescales of Appendix G. We replace all family-specific initializations with a shared τ=8\tau=8, corresponding to λf=e−1/8\lambda_{f}=e^{-1/8}. Test nMAE and nRMSE remain essentially unchanged from Table 2 across all four protocols.

To examine whether training recovers the same persistence parameters from the two initializations, we convert the learned λf\lambda_{f} back to an implied timescale,

τ^f=−1/logλf,\hat{\tau}_{f}=-1/\log\lambda_{f},

the inverse of the initialization λf=e−1/τf\lambda_{f}=e^{-1/\tau_{f}}. Table 23 reports these values for every latent-effect family.

The two initializations do not in general converge to a common set of timescales. Several families retain a strong dependence on their initialization, although some move substantially and others converge to similar values. Despite these different persistence solutions, forecast accuracy is nearly unchanged. Thus, on the real forecasting protocols, the supervised forecasting objective does not uniquely identify the family persistence parameters: multiple latent dynamics can support essentially the same predictive solution. The family-specific τf\tau_{f} should therefore be interpreted as an inductive bias rather than as a recovered physical timescale.

Section 5.4 and Appendix K test the same future-rollout mechanism on a matched leaky-integrator system. Starting from a shared initialization, the model recovers the correct persistence ordering λslow>λfast\lambda_{\mathrm{slow}}>\lambda_{\mathrm{fast}} and exhibits pathway-specific impulse responses. This provides a controlled capacity check under matched dynamics. On the four real forecasting protocols, different persistence configurations yield nearly identical forecast errors, so predictive accuracy alone does not establish identification of physical timescales.

Accordingly, BeliefGraph-JEPA does not rely on accurately specifying the physical family timescales to obtain its reported forecasting performance: replacing the family-specific initialization by the shared τ=8\tau=8 initialization yields essentially the same error.

Taken together, these ablations show that the reported forecasting gains are not tied to a narrow optimization recipe. Residual reliance remains small under different residual initialization and graph-base supervision, additional pre-context driver history is unnecessary, and forecast accuracy is robust to replacing family-specific persistence initialization with a shared timescale.

Appendix K Synthetic latent-dynamics diagnostics

Section 5.4, Figure 3, and Table 3 report a class-matched sanity check on a known instance of Eq. (2). This appendix specifies the leaky-integrator system, the probe protocol, and the full numerical tables, then examines a saturating tanh\tanh transition mismatch (Appendix K.4). The probes are the learned family persistences λf\lambda_{f} and the future-impulse map from each driver to each target. Results use seed 4242.

K.1 Matched-dynamics system

Three continuous drivers ufastu_{\mathrm{fast}}, uslowu_{\mathrm{slow}}, and unullu_{\mathrm{null}} update three latent-effect families. Two observed targets read a sparse gain:

zf,t+1=λf​zf,t+(1−λf)​αf​uparent⁡(f),t,yt=W​zt+εt.z_{f,t+1}=\lambda_{f}\,z_{f,t}+(1-\lambda_{f})\,\alpha_{f}\,u_{\mathrm{parent}(f),t},\qquad y_{t}=Wz_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}. (8)

Equation (8) is the continuous term of Eq. (2) with scalar (λf,αf)(\lambda_{f},\alpha_{f}) and delay d=0d{=}0. The ground-truth parameters are λfast=0.40\lambda_{\mathrm{fast}}=0.40, λslow=0.75\lambda_{\mathrm{slow}}=0.75, αfast=αslow=1\alpha_{\mathrm{fast}}=\alpha_{\mathrm{slow}}=1, and λnull=αnull=0\lambda_{\mathrm{null}}=\alpha_{\mathrm{null}}=0. WW maps the fast effect onto yfasty_{\mathrm{fast}} and the slow effect onto yslowy_{\mathrm{slow}}. The null family has no target edge. Observation noise is εt∼𝒩⁡(0,0.0152)\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.015^{2}). Drivers are a weak AR background with sparse pulses.

The instantaneous step gains are therefore (1−λ)​α=0.60(1-\lambda)\alpha=0.60 on the fast channel and 0.250.25 on the slow channel. Both step gains are large relative to the observation-noise scale, so neither pathway is hidden by noise; the two mechanisms are instead distinguished primarily by their persistence. A unit pulse on ufastu_{\mathrm{fast}} peaks at yfast=0.60y_{\mathrm{fast}}=0.60 and leaves yslow=0y_{\mathrm{slow}}=0; a unit pulse on uslowu_{\mathrm{slow}} peaks at yslow=0.25y_{\mathrm{slow}}=0.25 and leaves yfast=0y_{\mathrm{fast}}=0; a pulse on unullu_{\mathrm{null}} moves neither target. The typed prior supplied to the model is this ground-truth graph.

K.2 Identification protocol

Windows use context LX=8L_{X}=8, horizon H=32H=32, and a 6464-step latent warmup. All but the last context target are zeroed. Superscript id\mathrm{id} marks this identification setting: graph variants use the hard-bottleneck fusion of Section 5.2 (graph-covered driver tokens are withheld from the direct path), family states enter at γf≡1\gamma_{f}{\equiv}1, and each λf\lambda_{f} is a scalar initialized at 0.5750.575, the midpoint of (0.40,0.75)(0.40,0.75). Correct ranking therefore requires the two persistences to move in opposite directions. FRid (HB) is future latent-effect rollout under that fusion.

The ladder is DCid, future-driver tokens without a graph; IEid, an instant graph with λf≡0\lambda_{f}{\equiv}0; RBid and RB-GRid, a current recurrent belief without and with graph-first residual routing; FRid (HB) and FR-GRid, future latent-effect rollout without and with that routing. Architecture and optimization follow Appendix G (width 128128, batch 1616, learning rate 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4}, 4040 epochs). Results are seed 4242. The training split has 9696 sessions of length 384384.

After training, two probes are read from the checkpoint. The first is the learned (λfast,λslow)(\lambda_{\mathrm{fast}},\lambda_{\mathrm{slow}}) and whether λslow>λfast\lambda_{\mathrm{slow}}>\lambda_{\mathrm{fast}}. The second is a unit future pulse on one driver with a zero context: the reported impulse Id→yI_{d\to y} is the maximum absolute response of target yy over the horizon. The ground-truth on-path step gains are 0.600.60 and 0.250.25; off-path entries are the crosstalk and the null driver.

K.3 Results

Figure 3 and Table 3 summarize learned persistences and future-pulse responses for the current-belief and rollout variants. Tables 24–25 report the full identification ladder.

The no-rollout variants fail to recover horizon-dependent responses to future driver pulses. DCid, IEid, RBid, and RB-GRid all record MAE 0.0630.063, with yfasty_{\mathrm{fast}} MAE 0.0770.077 and yslowy_{\mathrm{slow}} MAE 0.0490.049, and all four produce zero future-pulse responses. IEid fixes λf≡0\lambda_{f}{\equiv}0, and the two current-belief models leave the persistences nearly equal (λ≈0.62\lambda{\approx}0.62–0.640.64) rather than separating the fast and slow families. DCid receives future-driver tokens directly, but likewise produces zero pulse responses. Thus, under this identification protocol, direct future conditioning alone does not recover the latent future driver-response dynamics.

The current graph belief HtGH_{t}^{G} is computed at the forecast anchor and remains fixed over the prediction horizon. A driver pulse introduced at lead time hh therefore never updates ZFZ^{F} in the current-belief variants, so λf\lambda_{f} receives no gradient that identifies how later driver effects should persist across future horizons. This is why RBid and RB-GRid match on every probe.

Future rollout changes this identification path. Applying Zt+hF=ℱ⁡(Zt+h−1F,Dt+h−1)Z_{t+h}^{F}=\mathcal{F}(Z_{t+h-1}^{F},D_{t+h-1}) at every lead time causes a later driver pulse to enter Zt+hFZ_{t+h}^{F} and propagate across subsequent horizons under λf\lambda_{f}. FRid (HB) moves λfast\lambda_{\mathrm{fast}} from 0.5750.575 to 0.4490.449 and λslow\lambda_{\mathrm{slow}} from 0.5750.575 to 0.6410.641, recovering the correct persistence ordering and reducing MAE from 0.0630.063 to 0.0310.031. Its fast-path pulse response rises to 0.3710.371 versus the ground-truth 0.600.60, with only 0.0100.010 crosstalk onto yslowy_{\mathrm{slow}}. That gain is confined to the fast target: MAE falls from 0.0770.077 to 0.0130.013, while the slow-path pulse stays at 00 and yslowy_{\mathrm{slow}} MAE remains 0.0490.049.

Graph-first residual routing recovers the remaining pathway. FR-GRid moves the learned persistences to 0.4290.429 and 0.6790.679, closer to the ground-truth (0.40,0.75)(0.40,0.75), reduces overall MAE to 0.0130.013, and lowers the two per-target MAEs to 0.0130.013 and 0.0140.014. The corresponding future-pulse responses are 0.4300.430 on the fast wired path and 0.1410.141 on the slow wired path, while off-path crosstalk remains 0.0080.008 and the null-driver response 0.0020.002. Thus, under matched dynamics, the rollout variants recover the correct persistence ordering, while the full FR-GRid model exhibits pathway-specific responses on both wired paths.

K.4 Saturating tanh\tanh mismatch

The matched system in Eq. (8) uses the same linear leaky integrator as the model. To test a mild class mismatch we keep (λf,αf)(\lambda_{f},\alpha_{f}), d≡0d{\equiv}0, observation noise, drivers, and the typed prior fixed, and replace the latent update by z←tanh⁡(λ​z+(1−λ)​α​u)z\leftarrow\tanh\bigl(\lambda z+(1-\lambda)\alpha u\bigr). A unit pulse then peaks at tanh⁡(0.60)≈0.537\tanh(0.60)\approx 0.537 on yfasty_{\mathrm{fast}} and tanh⁡(0.25)≈0.245\tanh(0.25)\approx 0.245 on yslowy_{\mathrm{slow}}. The trained model remains the linear integrator of Eq. (2). Optimization and initialization follow Appendix K.2 (width 128128, batch 1616, learning rate 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4}, seed 4242, α\alpha initialized at 0.50.5). The identification ladder is trained for 4040 epochs, matching the linear system; the last row trains the same FR-GRid recipe for 8080 epochs.

Tables 26–27 report the same probes as the matched system.

Without future rollout the 4040-epoch probes match the linear system: DCid, IEid, RBid, and RB-GRid leave MAE at 0.0440.044 and produce no future-pulse response, and the current-belief persistences stay near 0.620.62–0.640.64. Unlike the matched system, FRid (HB) also stays near the initialization (0.5800.580, 0.5910.591), does not recover the rank, and records zero pulse responses. At 4040 epochs, FR-GRid separates the persistences (0.401<0.6090.401<0.609) and halves MAE to 0.0230.023 by fitting the fast target (0.0130.013), but yslowy_{\mathrm{slow}} MAE remains 0.0340.034 and the slow-path pulse is 0.0010.001 against the saturated peak 0.2450.245. The fast-path pulse is 0.2780.278 against 0.5370.537, with 0.0080.008 crosstalk.

At 8080 epochs the same FR-GRid recipe recovers both wired pathways: the slow-path pulse rises to 0.1260.126, the fast-path pulse to 0.3300.330, and the two per-target MAEs both fall to 0.0120.012. The learned persistences are then 0.3430.343 and 0.6150.615, still farther from (0.40,0.75)(0.40,0.75) than the 4040-epoch matched estimates (0.4290.429, 0.6790.679).

Appendix L Typed-graph generation prompt

Cursor Grok 4.6 [46] is queried once per dataset, offline. PreDist receives a second query that tags each edge dyn\mathrm{dyn} or alg\mathrm{alg}. The input is the schema, variable descriptions, and the constraints below. The output is a JSON graph that is checked against a fixed schema, reviewed, and frozen; training loads that file and never calls the model. Self-loops and reverse message-passing edges are added programmatically after the proposal. Listing 1 is the shared instruction. Dataset-specific node inventories and routing constraints follow. CGMacros and Shanghai Diabetes use the same shared instruction with a single glucose target; their frozen prompts are stored with the graphs.

VitalDB. Intraoperative vitals on a regularly sampled grid: MBP, HR, SpO2, BIS. Dense continuous actions: propofol and remifentanil pump rates. No exogenous variables.

Greenhouse. Indoor climate on a 5 min grid: Tair, Rhair, CO2air, PARin. Dense continuous actions: Tpipe, VentLee, VentWind, AssimLight, EnScr, BlckScr, CO2dosing. All eight outdoor-weather channels stay on the direct path; only Tout, Windsp, PARout, and AbsHumOut are graph exo nodes.

Wastewater nutrient control. Tank-1 nutrient state on a 2 min grid: DO, NH4, PO4. Continuous actions: metal-salt dosing and blower factor. Categorical actions: inlet and outlet process phases. Exogenous: inflow and water temperature; both are graph exo nodes.

PreDist. Substation thermodynamics on a 10 min grid. Continuous actions: valve position and supply-temperature setpoint. Categorical actions: pump status, control mode, three-way valve. Exogenous: outdoor temperature and primary-grid supply temperature. Temperatures are inertial (dyn\mathrm{dyn}); heat power and flow are algebraic (alg\mathrm{alg}). A second query, given the same nodes, tags every edge with timescale dyn\mathrm{dyn} or alg\mathrm{alg} and uses a disjoint relation vocabulary.
